title: Strongly Connected Components
tagline: Collapse mutually-reachable groups in a digraph — Kosaraju and Tarjan.

intuition.analogy: In a city of one-way streets, a strongly connected component is a neighbourhood where you can drive from any corner to any other and back. Different neighbourhoods may only connect one way.
paragraphs: A strongly connected component (SCC) of a directed graph is a maximal set of vertices where every vertex can reach every other. Condensing each SCC into a single node turns any digraph into a DAG — extremely useful for 2-SAT, dependency analysis, and DP.

Kosaraju's method is two DFS passes: first record finish times, then DFS the transposed graph in decreasing finish order; each tree is one SCC. The transpose trick ensures you can't 'leak' out of a component.
Tarjan's method finds SCCs in a single DFS using discovery times and low-link values, popping a component off a stack whenever a node's low-link equals its own index. Both are linear time.
intuition.keyIdea: Order vertices by DFS finish time, then explore the reverse graph — each reverse-DFS tree is exactly one SCC.

steps.title: First DFS (Kosaraju)
steps.detail: Run DFS on the original graph, pushing each vertex onto a stack when it finishes.

steps.title: Transpose
steps.detail: Reverse every edge to build the transposed graph.

steps.title: Second DFS
steps.detail: Pop vertices from the stack; for each unvisited one, DFS the transpose. Every vertex reached forms one SCC.

complexity.timeReason: Two linear DFS passes (Kosaraju) or one (Tarjan).
complexity.spaceReason: Adjacency, transpose, stack, and component arrays.

pitfalls: Kosaraju needs the transpose; forgetting to reverse edges breaks correctness.
Recursion depth can be large — iterative DFS for big graphs.
Tarjan's low-link update rules (tree edge vs back edge vs on-stack) are subtle — get them exactly right.

dryRun.clickMoment: {0,1,2} are mutually reachable (a cycle), and {3,4} form another. The edge 2→3 connects them only one way, so they stay separate components in the condensation DAG.
